content.title: Daily Execution Loop: How to Build a Daily Execution Routine
content.definition: A daily execution loop is a fixed routine that turns a plan into finished work every day: pick one priority in the morning, protect a block of time for it, check in when it is done and close the day with a two-line record of what moved and what comes first tomorrow. It replaces motivation with a repeatable sequence.

question_sections.question: What are the steps of a daily execution loop?
question_sections.answer: Four steps: choose one priority before opening email, book a protected block for it, mark it done or note the blocker at a fixed check-in, and close the day by writing tomorrow's first action. The loop is complete only when the close is written.

question_sections.question: How long should daily execution routines take?
question_sections.answer: The planning and closing steps take 5-10 minutes combined. The protected block is 60-90 minutes of focused work on the one priority. Planning that takes longer than that is a sign of overplanning.

question_sections.question: What if you miss a day?
question_sections.answer: Restart with the next morning's step, not a catch-up list. One missed day is normal; the rule is never miss twice, and on a low-energy day run a minimum viable day: one small action that keeps the loop alive.

facts: Planning plus close: 5-10 minutes a day; protected block: 60-90 minutes.
Three recovery rules: no catch-up, never miss twice, minimum viable day.

content.title: Reset Cycle: What the Reset Cycle Model Is and How to Break It
content.definition: The reset cycle is the pattern of starting a plan at full intensity, missing a day or two, deciding the plan is ruined and restarting from scratch weeks later. The reset cycle model breaks it by making restarts small and immediate: no catch-up, never miss twice, and a minimum viable day when energy is low.

question_sections.question: What causes a reset cycle?
question_sections.answer: All-or-nothing plans. When a plan only counts if every day is perfect, one miss makes the whole plan feel failed, so waiting for a fresh start - Monday, next month, January - seems like the rational move.

question_sections.question: How do you break the reset cycle?
question_sections.answer: Restart the next day at minimum size instead of waiting for a clean start. Drop the backlog (no catch-up), allow one miss but never two, and define a minimum viable day: the smallest action that keeps the plan alive.

question_sections.question: What is a cycle reset versus a full reset?
question_sections.answer: A cycle reset restarts the routine the next day without changing the plan; a full reset throws the plan away and starts over. The model keeps cycle resets cheap so that full resets become unnecessary.

facts: Three rules: no catch-up, never miss twice, minimum viable day.
A restart happens the next scheduled day, not the next Monday or month.
The Spry / BHPC operating system builds these rules into its daily protocol ($49, one-time).

faq.question: What is the reset cycle?
faq.answer: The reset cycle is the loop of starting hard, missing a day, declaring the plan ruined and restarting from zero later. It feels like a motivation problem but is a plan-design problem: the plan has no rule for a missed day.

faq.question: What is a reset model?
faq.answer: A reset model is a rule set for what happens after you fall off a plan. The reset cycle model says: restart tomorrow, small, without catching up.

faq.question: What does cycle reset mean?
faq.answer: A cycle reset means restarting a routine at the next scheduled point - the next morning or the next week - rather than starting the entire plan over.

content.title: Phone Vortex Meaning: Protect Your Attention From Your Phone
content.definition: Phone vortex means the pull of a smartphone that turns a quick check into twenty minutes of scrolling, notifications and app-switching, leaving the original task untouched. Protecting attention from it is an environment problem rather than a willpower problem: change where the phone is, what can interrupt you and when you are allowed to check it.

question_sections.question: Why does a phone become a vortex?
question_sections.answer: Feeds and notifications run on variable rewards: you never know what the next refresh brings, so stopping always feels premature. Each check also breaks your focus, so returning to deep work costs several minutes every time.

question_sections.question: How do you get out of the phone vortex?
question_sections.answer: Put the phone out of reach during your protected work block, turn off every notification that is not from a person, batch checks to fixed times such as on the hour, and keep a paper note for the urge to look something up.

question_sections.question: What should you do the moment you notice it?
question_sections.answer: Put the phone face down in another room and write the next physical action of the task you left. Do not try to recover the lost time; restart a 25-minute block.

facts: Batch phone checks to fixed times, for example on the hour.
Keep the phone out of reach for the whole protected block (60-90 minutes).
The Spry / BHPC daily protocol builds the protected block into each day ($49, one-time).

faq.question: What does phone vortex mean?
faq.answer: Phone vortex describes how a quick phone check spirals into scrolling, notifications and app-switching that swallow time and attention. The fix is environmental: distance from the phone and fixed checking times.

faq.question: Is a phone vortex the same as doomscrolling?
faq.answer: Doomscrolling is one form of it, centred on negative news. A phone vortex is broader: any loop of checks, notifications and apps that pulls you away from what you meant to do.
